Please enter a professional email address.

SUBSCRIBE TO INSIGHTS

Asia Pacific real estate is often seen as a key diversifier – a region where different markets move on different cycles, offering access to some of the fastest-growing economies in the world. That view is still right, but the way returns are made and value is created in Asia have changed materially. With interest rates structurally higher, financing becoming more expensive and cross-border capital more selective, our approach is no longer simply to own the right property in the right city but also to lean deliberately into the structural themes reshaping the region. Put simply, the source of returns has moved from the market to the manager: less about holding the right asset and waiting, and more about actively transforming what we own.
When we sit down with investors today, six themes come up in almost every conversation: geopolitical instability, persistent inflation, elevated interest rates, shifting global trade patterns, volatile commodity prices, and the growing impact of AI on how businesses use space. Together, these themes have created a very different investing environment than the one that shaped a generation of real estate returns. That environment rewards a specific kind of investor – one that combines scale, local presence, sector expertise and, importantly, the ability to move across real estate, private equity, infrastructure and credit.
This reflects a wider evolution in how we invest across KKR Real Estate. Our philosophy rests on three capabilities that few managers can bring together in Asia. The first is the ability to draw on insights across asset classes – private equity, credit, infrastructure and macro – which lets us see structural change earlier and underwrite it with greater conviction. The second is deep operating expertise, delivered through captive, on-the-ground platforms that let us actively create value rather than wait for the market. The third is the scale to deploy with discipline across the capital stack, committing when capital is scarce and the best relative value is on offer. Insight, operating expertise and scale are the lens through which we assess every market and every deal that follows in this piece.
The Macro Backdrop: Higher Rates, Resilient Fundamentals
The market entered 2026 expecting interest rates to fall broadly across Asia. That is not what has happened. Japan has clearly exited its zero-interest-rate policy and continues to raise rates gradually; the yen and long-term Japanese government bonds remain volatile. The Reserve Bank of Australia has raised rates three times already this year as domestic inflation reaccelerated. The Bank of Korea has signaled it is prepared to act if inflation stays high. The U.S. Fed, meanwhile, has paused, not pivoted – holding rates steady rather than cutting. The takeaway: the cheap financing that powered the last cycle is not coming back on the timeline many expected. Yet the underlying fundamentals – occupancy, rents, and tenant demand – have stayed resilient, which is why we see this as a repricing of capital, not a deterioration of the assets themselves.
EXHIBIT 1: APAC Policy Rates Diverging – Higher for Longer

Source: KKR Global Macro & Asset Allocation, Federal Reserve, Bank of Japan, Bank of Korea, RBA, Haver. As of June 2026 (Q2 2026 actuals).

The implication is clear: we can no longer rely on falling financing costs or cap-rate compression to do the work. Returns increasingly have to come from structural NOI growth and operational value creation. Encouragingly, transaction markets have adjusted rather than seized up. According to Jones Lang LaSalle’s Asia Pacific Capital Tracker, regional commercial real estate investment volumes hit USD 47.0 billion in Q1 2026 – up 31% year-on-year and the strongest first quarter on record.¹
EXHIBIT 2: APAC CRE Investment Volumes – Annual by Market (2021–2025)

Source: JLL Asia Pacific Capital Tracker (2021–2025); MSCI Real Capital Analytics; KKR analysis. Full-year direct investment volumes.

Two signals matter to us. First, Japan continues to anchor regional liquidity, supported by deep domestic institutional capital and a re-opening of debt markets. Second, higher rates are working through corporate balance sheets gradually rather than triggering a sudden crisis – exactly the environment in which our best opportunities emerge. Preqin's 2026 outlook adds a related point: dry powder relative to AUM is falling globally, a signal that complex, less capital-intensive strategies will become more valuable precisely because they are scarce.²
Japan: The Corporate Carve-Out Decade
Japan is our highest-conviction market in Asia, and where the thesis has evolved most. If the last cycle was about inflation returning and the Bank of Japan cautiously raising rates back toward normal, this cycle, in our view, is about corporate Japan’s economic renaissance itself.
Governance reforms driven by the Tokyo Stock Exchange, the government’s corporate-value guidelines (from its Ministry of Economy, METI) and a growing pressure from activist shareholders are motivating Japanese companies to improve capital efficiency, simplify balance sheets and focus on core businesses. This has contributed to a growing trend of conglomerates shedding real estate they have held for decades. JLL estimates the stock of corporate-held real estate in Japan at approximately ¥820 trillion (roughly USD 5.1 trillion) – more than ten times the actively-traded universe.³ Historically, this real estate has been managed to house a company’s own operations rather than to earn a return, which in many cases have left these assets under-invested, under-rented and under-managed.
EXHIBIT 3: Japan – Corporate-Held Real Estate Dwarfs the Traded Market

Source: JLL Japan Corporate Real Estate, June 2026; KKR analysis. Investable universe estimated at ~10% of total.

For investors with experience in corporate carve-outs and operating businesses, this creates an attractive opportunity set. Increasingly, our focus in Japan has evolved beyond acquiring individual assets to investing in operating businesses where real estate forms a strategic part of the platform. In many cases, we see opportunities to enhance operational performance, optimize portfolios and unlock value over time.
Another important structural development is the return of moderate inflation. The latest Shunto (Japan’s annual spring wage negotiations) delivered wage growth above 5% for a third consecutive year, well above the ~2% historical average, and it is beginning to show up in rents. Rents on prime offices are rising roughly 4%, supported by record-low vacancy, with multifamily rents following.⁴
EXHIBIT 4: Japan – Structural Wage Growth Above 5% is Feeding Rental Growth

Source: Japan Trade Union Confederation (Rengo) Shunto Results; KKR GMAA. 2026 figure as of April 10, 2026.

One example is Sapporo Real Estate, a corporate carve-out we signed in the past year, which includes Yebisu Garden Place, one of Tokyo's most recognizable mixed-use properties. Since we acquired the asset, we have worked closely with management to prepare its next phase as an independent company, including reviewing its operations, organizational priorities, and leasing strategy. Even in the early stages, we have seen encouraging results. A number of lease renewals have been completed at appropriate market levels, reflecting the strength of the asset and improving market fundamentals.
A key differentiator is KKR Japan Realty Management (KJRM), a real estate manager we acquired with our balance sheet, which manages two listed Japan REITs. As a dedicated Japan real estate management and operating platform with local teams on the ground, KJRM provides execution capability at scale and, combined with KKR's broader corporate relationships and the support of our private equity and infrastructure businesses, gives us a strong vantage point on where value can be created – an edge that few traditional real estate investors can replicate.
Korea: From Oversupply to Scarcity
Elsewhere in North Asia, we continue to see attractive opportunities in Korea. Following a period of post-pandemic oversupply, logistics fundamentals have improved meaningfully. New supply is moderating, while demand continues to be supported by one of the highest e-commerce penetration rates in Asia Pacific at approximately 41%.⁵
EXHIBIT 5: Korea – Post-COVID Oversupply Has Cleared; Pipeline Dropping Off

Source: CBRE Research (Greater Seoul Logistics), August 2025; JLL forecast; KKR analysis.

We see two forces converging. E-commerce continues to drive demand for logistics space, while construction costs have risen by roughly 25–30% since 2020 and tightening financing conditions have slowed new developments.⁶ Over the past two years, Korea has been one of the most resilient APAC markets: investment volumes remained above USD 20 billion annually through 2023–2025 despite higher rates, supported by large new commitments from Korean LPs that restored liquidity as foreign capital stepped back.⁷
For an investor with capital and operational capability, this creates a favorable medium-term opportunity, such as buying high-quality, recently built assets from under-capitalized owners at reset valuations, which benefit from an increasingly institutional demand base. We are also seeing a growing pipeline of corporate-originated opportunities in Korea, where combining real estate expertise with KKR's private equity and in-house operating capabilities creates a differentiated angle. We benefit from the expertise of our affiliated Korea asset manager, Kreate Asset Management, which enables us to underwrite opportunities with more conviction and execute the operational value creation that a purely capital-led approach cannot do.
Australia: Selective, Structural, Specialized
Australia is a market where we are highly selective. Inflation has remained above the RBA's target range, resulting in further rate increases during 2026. While domestic investors have generally adopted a more cautious stance, we are seeing continued interest from international capital seeking to invest through the cycle.⁸
EXHIBIT 6: Australia – Demand-Supply Mismatch Underpins Living Sectors

Source: Australian Bureau of Statistics; KKR analysis.

The long-term picture is what keeps our conviction high. Population growth continues to run at multiples of most developed-market peers, and high construction costs have materially reduced future supply across housing and industrial. We are focused on specialty living sectors – student accommodation and other segments within the living sector which are typically underserved by traditional rental developers – and continue to see opportunities in cold-storage logistics platforms where capital-constrained owners are selling into a market with very low vacancy and few new competitors.
Our Playbook for a Higher-Rate World
Our strategy has three distinct but reinforcing thematic buckets: flow, opportunistic and corporate. Flow investments come from repeatable sourcing channels – our operating platforms, long-standing broker and developer relationships, and sector businesses we already own. Opportunistic situations arise where market dislocation, capital-structure pressure or execution complexity narrows the pool of potential buyers. Corporate situations – the area we spend most of our time on today – are large-scale carve-outs, strategic divestitures and acquisitions of operating businesses that own real estate.
All three share a single conviction: in a higher-rate world, embedded value in under-managed portfolios and supply-constrained sectors is worth more than a lower cap rate on a stabilized asset. Unlocking that value takes a full toolkit – sector expertise, operating platforms, and the ability to bring in colleagues from private equity, credit, infrastructure and capital markets.
Our recent investment in leading data center platform STT GDC is a good example. Data centers are one of the most competitive sectors globally, and the opportunity offered a proven operating platform, a strong management team, established hyperscaler relationships and integrated development capability under one roof. We pursued it alongside KKR's Infrastructure team, showing how our Real Assets platform is designed to work – Real Estate and Infrastructure collaborating to reduce execution risk and expand the range of ways we can create value.
In our view, leaning into these structural themes – with the platforms, people and cross-firm capabilities to execute – is what will define the next generation of returns in Asia real estate. This is not a market that rewards the passive owner. It rewards the investor with a clear view of where structural value sits and the operational capability to unlock it. Put simply, it is a market for insight, operating expertise and scale – and for the manager able to bring all three to bear.

REFERENCES
¹ JLL, "Asia Pacific commercial real estate investment surges to record USD 47.0 billion in Q1 2026," 19 May 2026.
² Preqin, "Real Estate in 2026 – Global Report," December 2025.
³ JLL, Japan Corporate Real Estate estimates, June 2026.
⁴ CBRE, "Macro and Market Overview," November 2025; Japan Trade Union Confederation (Rengo) Shunto Results, April 2026.
⁵ CBRE Research, APAC E-commerce Penetration, August 2025.
⁶ Turner & Townsend International Construction Market Survey, March 2026.
⁷ CBRE Asia Pacific Investment Trends (Q1 2024 through Q1 2026); JLL Asia Pacific Capital Tracker (2023–2026). Korea annual investment volumes have averaged approximately USD 21 billion over 2023–2025.
⁸ CBRE, "Pacific Market Outlook," April 2026.

Insights / Research / Charts of the Week: Bitcoin Enters the Goldilocks Zone

Written by:

Alex Thorn
Head of Firmwide Research

Marc Hochstein
Vice President and Editor, Research

Topics

Bitcoin

research • August 21, 2026

Charts of the Week: Bitcoin Enters the Goldilocks Zone

This article originally appeared in Galaxy Research's weekly newsletter. Subscribe to get timely insights delivered to your inbox every Friday morning. Where is bitcoin now in the cycle? A useful exercise is to compare the spot price over time to three broad categories of models: ceiling models (typically based on long-term moving averages), which identify bull peaks when the market is extended above the historical trend; cost-basis models, which use onchain data to estimate whether current holders are in profit (and hence their motivation to sell, depending on how long they’ve held); and floor models, which detect when selling pressure exhausts. Looking back over more than a decade and a half, every major market top (2013, 2017-18, 2021) saw the price touch or break the dashed ceiling models. Every major crash found support near the dotted floors.

This week BTC ripped through the 200-week moving average floor and through the shorter-period Pi Cycle (111-day simple moving average) and short-term holder realized price cost bases. As of Thursday morning, bitcoin is now trading above all the floors and cost bases but well below the ceiling indicators. The implication is that capitulation is over. Holders are in profit across cohorts (no forced selling from underwater positions), and the price has room to run. Not necessarily the bottom, but possibly close.
